q: When two bodies at different temperatures are placed in contact, thermal energy flows on its own from the body with the:
o: Greater internal energy to the one with less internal energy
Larger mass to the one with smaller mass
Higher temperature to the one at lower temperature
Higher specific heat to the one with lower specific heat
x: Heat flows spontaneously from a region of higher temperature to a region of lower temperature. A body with more internal energy (for example a large cold object) can still be at the lower temperature.

q: Two bodies in contact are said to be in thermal equilibrium when they have the same:
x: Thermal equilibrium means there is no net flow of heat between the bodies, which happens when their temperatures are equal. Their internal energies and specific heats can still be very different.

q: A hot steel spoon at 60 °C is pushed into a large block of ice at −5 °C. The block has far more internal energy than the spoon. Heat flows:
o: From the ice to the spoon, because the ice has more internal energy
From the spoon to the ice, because the spoon is at a higher temperature
In neither direction, because their internal energies balance
From the ice to the spoon, because the ice has a larger mass
x: The direction of heat flow is decided by temperature, not by the total internal energy or mass. The spoon is hotter, so heat flows from the spoon into the ice.

q: Body X is in thermal equilibrium with body Y, and body Y is in thermal equilibrium with body Z. Which statement is correct?
o: X and Z are at the same temperature
X and Z must have the same internal energy
Heat will flow from X to Z when they touch
x: X and Y have the same temperature and Y and Z have the same temperature, so X and Z are at the same temperature and no heat flows between them. Equal temperature does not mean equal internal energy.

q: A hot body and a cold body are placed in contact inside a perfectly insulated box until they reach a common temperature. Which statement is correct?
o: The heat lost by the hot body equals the heat gained by the cold body
Both bodies change temperature by the same amount
The cold body gains more heat than the hot body loses
The final temperature is always the average of the two starting temperatures
x: With no heat lost to the surroundings, energy is conserved: heat lost by the hot body = heat gained by the cold body. The temperature changes are equal only if the two bodies have equal heat capacities.

q: 1 kg of water at 90 °C is mixed with 2 kg of water at 30 °C in an insulated container. Ignoring heat losses, the final temperature of the mixture is:
x: Heat lost = heat gained: 1 × c × (90 − T) = 2 × c × (T − 30), so 90 − T = 2T − 60 and T = 50 °C. 60 °C is the simple average, which ignores the unequal masses.

q: In physics, heat is best described as:
o: The total kinetic energy of all the molecules of a body
A measure of how hot or cold a body is
The energy a body holds because of its mass
Energy transferred from one body to another because of a temperature difference
x: Heat is energy in transit due to a temperature difference. The total molecular energy of a body is its internal energy, and 'how hot a body is' describes temperature.

q: A clinical thermometer placed under a patient's tongue for a minute shows the patient's body temperature because:
o: The thermometer reaches thermal equilibrium with the body
The thermometer stores the heat of the body permanently
Heat keeps flowing into the thermometer as long as it is in the mouth
The mercury has a higher temperature than the body
x: After a short time no net heat flows between the thermometer and the body, so both are at the same temperature and the reading equals body temperature.

q: Body X (mass 1 kg, specific heat 400 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 100 °C is placed in contact with body Y (mass 1 kg, specific heat 800 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 10 °C in an insulated box. The common final temperature is:
x: 400(100 − T) = 800(T − 10) gives 40 000 + 8000 = 1200T, so T = 40 °C. 70 °C comes from swapping the two specific heats; 55 °C is the plain average.

q: According to the kinetic theory, the temperature of a gas is a measure of the:
o: Total potential energy of its molecules
Average translational kinetic energy of its molecules
Total number of molecules in the container
x: Absolute temperature is proportional to the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules. Heat flows from higher to lower temperature, i.e. from faster-moving molecules on average to slower ones.

q: The SI unit of specific heat is:
x: Specific heat is the heat per kilogram per kelvin, so its unit is J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is the unit of molar specific heat, and J K⁻¹ is the unit of heat capacity.

q: The main difference between specific heat and molar specific heat of a substance is that molar specific heat refers to:
o: One gram of the substance instead of one kilogram
A rise of 1 °C instead of 1 K
One mole of the substance instead of one kilogram
x: Specific heat is the heat needed per kilogram per kelvin; molar specific heat is the heat needed per mole per kelvin. A change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K, so that is not the difference.

q: A substance has specific heat c and molar mass M (in kg mol⁻¹). Its molar specific heat C is given by:
x: One mole has a mass of M kilograms, so the heat per mole per kelvin is M times the heat per kilogram per kelvin: C = Mc.

q: The specific heat of water is 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and its molar mass is 0.018 kg mol⁻¹. The molar specific heat of water is about:
x: C = Mc = 0.018 × 4200 = 75.6 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Dividing instead of multiplying gives about 2.3 × 10⁵.

q: Helium has a molar specific heat at constant volume of 12.5 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and a molar mass of 0.004 kg mol⁻¹. Its specific heat at constant volume is:
x: c = C/M = 12.5/0.004 = 3125 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. 0.05 comes from multiplying by the molar mass instead of dividing.

q: 2 mol of a gas with molar specific heat at constant volume 20 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is heated at constant volume through 10 K. The heat supplied is:
x: Q = nCvΔT = 2 × 20 × 10 = 400 J. 200 J forgets the number of moles.

q: Two different molar specific heats (at constant volume and at constant pressure) are defined for a gas but are not usually needed for a solid because:
o: A gas expands much more on heating, so the heat needed depends strongly on the conditions
A gas has no definite mass
A solid cannot be heated at constant pressure
The molar mass of a gas changes when it is heated
x: When a gas is heated at constant pressure it expands a lot and does work, so it needs more heat than at constant volume. Solids and liquids expand very little, so the two values are almost equal.

q: The specific heat of copper is 400 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. If the mass of a copper sample is doubled, its specific heat becomes:
x: Specific heat is a property of the material, not of the sample size, so it stays 400 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. The heat needed for a given temperature rise doubles, but that is the heat capacity.

q: Hydrogen (molar mass 2 g mol⁻¹) and oxygen (molar mass 32 g mol⁻¹) have the same molar specific heat at constant volume. The ratio of the specific heat of hydrogen to that of oxygen (per kilogram) is:
x: Specific heat c = C/M. With the same C, c is inversely proportional to molar mass: c(H₂)/c(O₂) = 32/2 = 16. One kilogram of hydrogen contains 16 times as many moles.

q: The heat capacity of a 0.5 kg block of aluminium (specific heat 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) is:
x: Heat capacity = mc = 0.5 × 900 = 450 J K⁻¹. Unlike specific heat, heat capacity depends on the mass of the body.

q: A gas expands at constant pressure P, and its volume increases by ΔV. The work done by the gas is:
x: Work done by the gas = force × distance = (PA) × Δy = PΔV, where AΔy is the change in volume.

q: A gas at a constant pressure of 2 × 10⁵ Pa expands from 1 × 10⁻³ m³ to 3 × 10⁻³ m³. The work done by the gas is:
x: W = PΔV = 2 × 10⁵ × (3 − 1) × 10⁻³ = 400 J. 600 J uses the final volume instead of the change in volume.

q: A gas is compressed at a constant pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa from 5 litres to 2 litres (1 litre = 10⁻³ m³). The work done on the gas is:
x: ΔV = 3 litres = 3 × 10⁻³ m³, so work done on the gas = PΔV = 1.0 × 10⁵ × 3 × 10⁻³ = 300 J. 3 × 10⁵ J forgets to convert litres to m³.

q: On a pressure–volume graph of a gas changing from one state to another, the work done by the gas is given by the:
o: Pressure at the final point multiplied by the final volume
Area between the curve and the volume axis
x: Work done = ∫P dV, which is the area under the P–V curve down to the volume axis. For constant pressure this area is the rectangle PΔV.

q: A gas is heated in a closed rigid steel cylinder, so its volume cannot change. The work done by the gas is:
o: Equal to the rise in pressure times the volume
x: Work done by a gas is PΔV. In a rigid container ΔV = 0, so no work is done even though the pressure rises.

q: When a gas in a cylinder is compressed by pushing the piston in, the work done by the gas is:
o: Positive, because energy is given to the gas
Zero, because the gas does not move
Always equal to the heat lost by the gas
x: Work done by the gas is PΔV and ΔV is negative in a compression, so the work done by the gas is negative; equivalently, positive work is done on the gas by the piston.

q: A gas in a cylinder at a constant pressure of 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa pushes a piston of area 0.02 m² outward through 0.1 m. The work done by the gas is:
x: ΔV = area × distance = 0.02 × 0.1 = 2 × 10⁻³ m³, so W = PΔV = 1.5 × 10⁵ × 2 × 10⁻³ = 300 J.

q: The product of pressure and volume, PV, has the same SI unit as:
x: Pa × m³ = N m⁻² × m³ = N m = J, the unit of energy and work. That is why PΔV gives work in joules.

q: 2 mol of an ideal gas is heated at constant pressure so that its temperature rises by 50 K. Taking R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, the work done by the gas is:
x: At constant pressure PΔV = nRΔT (from PV = nRT), so W = 2 × 8.3 × 50 = 830 J. 415 J forgets the 2 moles.

q: A gas expands at constant pressure and does work W. If the same change in volume took place at twice the pressure, the work done by the gas would be:
x: W = PΔV, so with ΔV unchanged the work is directly proportional to the pressure: doubling P doubles the work to 2W.

q: Let Q be the heat supplied to a gas, ΔU the increase in its internal energy and W the work done by the gas. The first law of thermodynamics is:
x: Heat supplied is used partly to raise internal energy and partly to do external work: Q = ΔU + W when W is the work done by the gas.

q: 500 J of heat is supplied to a gas and the gas does 200 J of work on its surroundings. The change in internal energy of the gas is:
x: With W as work done by the gas, ΔU = Q − W = 500 − 200 = +300 J, an increase.

q: 300 J of work is done on a gas while the gas gives out 100 J of heat to its surroundings. The change in internal energy of the gas is:
x: Energy in = 300 J of work done on the gas; energy out = 100 J of heat. ΔU = 300 − 100 = +200 J.

q: If Q is the heat supplied to a system and W is the work done on the system, the first law of thermodynamics is written as:
x: Both heat supplied and work done on the system add energy to it, so ΔU = Q + W in this convention. Q = ΔU + W is correct only when W is the work done by the system.

q: The internal energy of a fixed amount of an ideal gas depends only on its:
x: An ideal gas has no intermolecular forces, so its internal energy is just the kinetic energy of its molecules, which depends only on temperature.

q: A gas gives out 200 J of heat to its surroundings while its internal energy decreases by 500 J. The work done by the gas is:
x: Using Q = ΔU + W with W done by the gas: −200 = −500 + W, so W = +300 J. The gas does 300 J of work on the surroundings.

q: A gas does 400 J of work on its surroundings while its internal energy decreases by 150 J. During this process the gas:
x: Q = ΔU + W, with W the work done by the gas: Q = −150 + 400 = +250 J, so the gas absorbs 250 J. The 400 J of work comes from 250 J of heat plus 150 J of internal energy.

q: A gas is taken from state X to state Y by two different paths. Which quantity is the same for both paths?
o: Change in internal energy of the gas
Heat absorbed minus the change in internal energy
x: Internal energy is a function of state, so ΔU depends only on the initial and final states. Heat and work depend on the path; heat minus ΔU equals the work, which also depends on the path.

q: 600 J of heat is supplied to a gas kept at constant volume. The increase in the internal energy of the gas is:
x: At constant volume the gas does no work (W = PΔV = 0), so all the heat supplied goes into internal energy: ΔU = Q = 600 J.

q: An ideal gas expands adiabatically (no heat enters or leaves) and does work on a piston. Its temperature:
x: With Q = 0, the first law gives ΔU = −W (W done by the gas). The work is done at the expense of internal energy, so the internal energy and hence the temperature fall.

q: The first law of thermodynamics is a statement of the law of:
x: The first law says that heat supplied to a system is accounted for as increase in internal energy plus work done, i.e. energy is neither created nor destroyed.

q: An ideal gas expands isothermally and absorbs 250 J of heat. The work done by the gas is:
x: At constant temperature the internal energy of an ideal gas does not change (ΔU = 0), so Q = ΔU + W gives W = Q = 250 J of work done by the gas.

q: An inventor claims a machine that keeps doing useful work forever without taking in any energy. This is impossible because it would violate:
o: The law of conservation of energy
The law of conservation of mass
x: Work cannot come from nothing: by the first law, work done must be supplied by heat taken in or by a fall in internal energy, which cannot fall forever.

q: When a bicycle tyre is pumped up quickly, the barrel of the pump becomes warm. The main reason is that:
o: Heat flows into the air from the hand
Friction of the air molecules with each other creates new energy
Work done on the air in compressing it increases its internal energy
The air expands and gains heat from the surroundings
x: The rapid compression is nearly adiabatic, so the work done on the air goes into its internal energy and the air gets hotter, warming the pump. No energy is created.

q: A gas is taken through a complete cycle and returns to its starting state. In one cycle the net work done by the gas is 120 J. The net heat absorbed by the gas in the cycle is:
x: After a complete cycle the gas is back in the same state, so ΔU = 0. Then Q = ΔU + W gives net heat absorbed = net work done by the gas = 120 J.

q: A gas in a perfectly insulated cylinder is compressed, with 200 J of work done on it. What happens to its internal energy and temperature?
o: Internal energy is unchanged and temperature is unchanged
Internal energy falls by 200 J and temperature falls
Internal energy rises by 200 J and temperature rises
Internal energy rises by 200 J but temperature is unchanged
x: Insulation means Q = 0, so all 200 J of work done on the gas becomes internal energy (ΔU = +200 J). For a gas, a rise in internal energy means a rise in temperature.

q: A system exchanges neither heat nor work with its surroundings. According to the first law, its internal energy:
x: With Q = 0 and W = 0, the first law gives ΔU = 0. The energy of an isolated system is conserved.

q: Heat is supplied to a gas in a cylinder fitted with a freely moving piston, so the pressure stays constant. The heat supplied is used to:
o: Increase the internal energy and do work against the external pressure
Increase the pressure of the gas
x: At constant pressure the gas both warms up (ΔU increases) and expands, doing work PΔV. By conservation of energy Q = ΔU + PΔV.

q: In Joule's experiment, falling weights turn paddles in insulated water and the water's temperature rises. This shows that:
o: Heat can be destroyed by mechanical work
Water has a very low specific heat
Mechanical work can be converted into internal energy
Temperature does not depend on internal energy
x: The work done by the falling weights is converted into internal energy of the water, raising its temperature. This established heat and work as forms of energy transfer, the basis of the first law.

q: The specific heat of a substance is the heat required to raise the temperature of:
o: 1 mol of the substance by 1 K
1 kg of the substance by 1 K
1 kg of the substance from its melting point to its boiling point
x: Specific heat c is the heat needed per kilogram per kelvin, c = Q/(mΔT). For the whole body it is the heat capacity; for one mole it is the molar specific heat.

q: How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of 2 kg of water by 10 K? (Specific heat of water = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)
x: Q = mcΔT = 2 × 4200 × 10 = 84 000 J = 84 kJ. 42 kJ forgets the mass of 2 kg.

q: The molar specific heat of a gas at constant volume, Cv, is the heat needed to raise the temperature of:
o: 1 kg of the gas by 1 K at constant pressure
1 mol of the gas by 1 K at constant volume
1 mol of the gas by 1 K at constant pressure
1 kg of the gas by 1 K at constant volume
x: Cv refers to one mole, a 1 K rise and a fixed volume. One mole at constant pressure defines Cp; per kilogram gives the specific heat, not the molar value.

q: For a gas, the molar specific heat at constant pressure Cp is greater than Cv because at constant pressure:
o: The gas loses heat to the container
The internal energy rises more for the same temperature rise
Part of the heat supplied is used to do work as the gas expands
x: At constant pressure the gas expands and does work, so extra heat is needed beyond the rise in internal energy. The rise in internal energy for a given temperature rise is the same in both cases for an ideal gas.

q: A 0.5 kg metal block absorbs 9000 J of heat and its temperature rises by 20 K. The specific heat of the metal is:
x: c = Q/(mΔT) = 9000/(0.5 × 20) = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. 450 comes from multiplying by the mass instead of dividing.

q: Equal masses of water (specific heat 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) and copper (specific heat 420 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) receive the same amount of heat. The temperature rise of the copper is:
o: Ten times that of the water
Equal to that of the water
x: For the same Q and m, ΔT = Q/(mc) is inversely proportional to c. Copper's specific heat is one-tenth of water's, so its temperature rises ten times as much.

q: Water is used as the coolant in car engine radiators mainly because it:
o: Has a low specific heat, so it heats up quickly
Expands a great deal on heating
Has a high specific heat, so it absorbs much heat for a small rise in temperature
x: Water's high specific heat (about 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) means each kilogram carries away a lot of heat from the engine while its own temperature rises only a little.

q: Two identical samples of an ideal gas receive the same amount of heat, one at constant volume and the other at constant pressure. The rise in temperature is:
x: At constant volume all the heat goes into internal energy. At constant pressure part of it is used for work in expansion, so less goes into internal energy and the temperature rises less (Cp > Cv).

q: The heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 mol of a gas by 1 K while its pressure is kept constant is called its:
o: Molar specific heat at constant volume
Molar specific heat at constant pressure
x: This is the definition of Cp. At constant volume it would be Cv; per kilogram it would be a specific heat; for the whole body it would be the heat capacity.

q: For one mole of an ideal gas, the molar specific heats at constant pressure and constant volume are related by:
x: Applying the first law at constant pressure and constant volume gives Cp − Cv = R for an ideal gas, where R is the molar gas constant.

q: For an ideal gas Cv = 20.8 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Taking R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, its Cp is:
x: Cp = Cv + R = 20.8 + 8.3 = 29.1 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Subtracting R by mistake gives 12.5.

q: The ratio γ = Cp/Cv for an ideal gas is always:
x: Cp = Cv + R, so Cp is always larger than Cv and γ = Cp/Cv > 1.

q: In deriving Cp − Cv = R, the work PΔV done by n moles of an ideal gas heated at constant pressure through ΔT is replaced by:
x: From PV = nRT at constant pressure, PΔV = nRΔT. Then nCpΔT = nCvΔT + nRΔT, giving Cp − Cv = R.

q: In deriving Cp − Cv = R, the rise in internal energy when n moles of ideal gas are heated through ΔT at constant pressure is taken as nCvΔT. This is justified because:
o: The volume of the gas does not change
No work is done by the gas at constant pressure
Cp and Cv are equal for an ideal gas
The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature
x: For an ideal gas ΔU depends only on ΔT, so the same temperature rise gives the same ΔU = nCvΔT whatever the process. The volume does change at constant pressure, and work is done.

q: For an ideal gas Cp = 29.0 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Taking R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, the ratio γ = Cp/Cv is about:
x: Cv = Cp − R = 29.0 − 8.3 = 20.7 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, so γ = 29.0/20.7 ≈ 1.40. 0.71 is the inverse ratio Cv/Cp.

q: For a certain ideal gas Cv = 3R/2. Using Cp − Cv = R, the value of γ = Cp/Cv is:
x: Cp = 3R/2 + R = 5R/2, so γ = (5R/2)/(3R/2) = 5/3. 3/5 is the ratio upside down.

q: Physically, the difference Cp − Cv = R for an ideal gas is equal to:
o: The increase in internal energy of 1 mol when heated through 1 K
The heat needed to raise 1 mol by 1 K at constant volume
The work done by 1 mol when heated through 1 K at constant pressure
The kinetic energy of one molecule at 1 K
x: Heating 1 mol through 1 K needs extra heat at constant pressure only because the gas expands and does work PΔV = R × 1 K. The increase in internal energy is Cv, the same in both cases.

q: Treating both as ideal gases, how does the value of Cp − Cv (per mole) for hydrogen compare with that for oxygen?
o: It is the same for both
It is 16 times greater for hydrogen
It is 16 times greater for oxygen
It depends on the temperature of each gas
x: Per mole, Cp − Cv = R for every ideal gas, about 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, whatever the molar mass. Only the per-kilogram values would differ.

q: 2 mol of an ideal gas are heated through 10 K. Taking R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, how much more heat is needed at constant pressure than at constant volume?
x: Extra heat = n(Cp − Cv)ΔT = nRΔT = 2 × 8.3 × 10 = 166 J. This extra heat is the work done by the gas in expanding. 83 J forgets the 2 moles.
